Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 113, verses 1–2 (part 1 of 3):

Muslim related in his Sahih, from the report of Qays ibn Hazim, from Uqba ibn Amir, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Have you not seen verses that were revealed tonight, the like of which has never been seen: 'I seek refuge with the Lord of the daybreak' and 'I seek refuge with the Lord of mankind'?"

In another wording, from the narration of Muhammad ibn Ibrahim al-Taymi, from Uqba: that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: "Shall I not inform you of the best thing with which those who seek refuge have sought refuge?" I said: "Yes." He said: "Recite: 'I seek refuge with the Lord of the daybreak,' and recite: 'I seek refuge with the Lord of mankind.'"

In al-Tirmidhi: Qutayba told us, Ibn Lahi'a informed us, from Yazid ibn Abi Habib, from Ali ibn Rabah, from Uqba ibn Amir, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) commanded me to recite the two refuge surahs (al-Mu'awwidhatayn) after every prayer."

He said: This is a gharib (strange, weak-chain) hadith.

In al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i and Sunan Abi Dawud, from Abdullah ibn Habib, who said: "We went out on a night of rain and darkness, seeking the Prophet (ﷺ) so that he would lead us in prayer. We found him, and he said: 'Recite.' I said nothing. Then he said: 'Recite.' I said nothing. Then he said: 'Recite.' I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, what should I recite?' He said: 'Recite: "Say, He is Allah, One" and the two refuge surahs, when you enter the evening and when you enter the morning, three times, and they will suffice you against everything.'"

Al-Tirmidhi said: This is a hasan sahih (good, authentic) hadith.

Also in al-Tirmidhi, from the hadith of al-Jurayri, from Abu Hurayra, from Abu Sa'id, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to seek refuge from the jinn and the evil eye of humans, until the two refuge surahs were revealed. When they were revealed, he took them and left whatever was other than them." He said: And on this subject there is a report from Anas.

This is a gharib hadith.

In the Two Sahihs (al-Bukhari and Muslim), from Aisha: "that the Prophet (ﷺ), whenever he went to his bed, would blow into his palms with 'Say, He is Allah, One' and the two refuge surahs together, then wipe with them over his face and whatever his hands could reach of his body. Aisha said: When he fell ill, he would order me to do that for him."

I say: Thus Yunus narrated it from al-Zuhri, from Urwa, from Aisha. Al-Bukhari mentioned it.

Malik narrated it from al-Zuhri, from Urwa, from her: "that the Prophet (ﷺ), when he was ill, would recite over himself with the refuge (surahs) and blow. When his pain became severe, I would recite over him and wipe with his hand, seeking its blessing."

Likewise Ma'mar said, from al-Zuhri, from Urwa, from her: "that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to blow over himself with the refuge (surahs) during the illness in which he died. When he became heavy, I was the one who blew over him with them and wiped with his own hand for its blessing. I asked Ibn Shihab: How did he blow? He said: He blew on his hands, then wiped with them over his face." Al-Bukhari mentioned it also.

This is the correct view: that Aisha was doing this, and the Prophet (ﷺ) neither commanded her nor forbade her. As for it being that he sought ruqya (spiritual healing recitation) and asked her to perform it upon him, that is not so. Perhaps some narrators related it by meaning, and so they thought that because she did this and the Prophet (ﷺ) approved it, that he was commanding her. But there is a difference between the two matters. His approving her recitation over him does not necessitate that he himself was seeking ruqya. So the one is not the same as the other. Perhaps what he commanded her to do was only to wipe over himself with his hand. Thus he was the one reciting for himself, and since his hand had become too weak to move over all of his body, he ordered her to move it over his body. This would be different from her own recitation over him and her wiping over his body. So she did this and that. What he commanded her was only the moving of his hand, not his ruqya. And Allah knows best.

The purpose: the discussion concerns these two surahs, the explanation of their great benefit, and the intense need, indeed the necessity, for them. No one is ever free of need for them, and they have a particular effect in repelling magic, the evil eye, and all other evils. The servant's need to seek refuge with these two surahs is greater than his need for breath, food, drink and clothing. So we say, and Allah is the One sought for help:

The two surahs comprise three fundamentals, which are the fundamentals of seeking refuge:

First: the act of seeking refuge itself.
Second: that in which refuge is sought.
Third: that from which refuge is sought.

By knowing these, one recognizes the intense need and necessity for these two surahs.

So we establish three sections for them: Section One: on seeking refuge. Section Two: on the One in whom refuge is sought. Section Three: on that from which refuge is sought.

(Section One)

Know that the root "ʿ-w-dh" (ʿādha, "to seek refuge") and what is derived from it indicate guarding, shelter and deliverance. Its real meaning is fleeing from something you fear to one who protects you from it.

For this reason, the one in whom refuge is sought is called maʿādh (a place of refuge), just as he is called a refuge (malja'), and a stronghold (wizr).

In a hadith: "When the daughter of al-Jawn was brought in to the Prophet (ﷺ), he placed his hand upon her, and she said: 'I seek refuge with Allah from you.' He said to her: 'You have sought refuge with one who grants refuge. Return to your family.'"

So the meaning of ʿa'ūdhu ("I seek refuge") is: I take shelter, I hold fast, and I guard myself.

As to its origin, there are two opinions. The first: that it is derived from covering (satr). The second: that it is derived from clinging to proximity (luzūm al-mujāwara).

As for the one who said it is from covering, he said: The Arabs call the hollow beneath the tree in which one has hidden by it an ʿawwadh, with a damma on the ʿayn and a shadda on the waw, or with a fatha. So, as the one who seeks refuge takes shelter by the tree and hides by its base and shade, they named it ʿawwadh. Likewise the one who seeks refuge hides from his enemy by the one he has sought refuge with, and is concealed by him from him.

As for the one who said it is clinging to proximity, he said: The Arabs call the flesh that adheres to the bone and cannot be separated from it ʿawwadh, because it holds fast to it and clings to it. Likewise the one who seeks refuge clings to the one in whom he seeks refuge, holds fast to him, and sticks to him.

Both opinions are true, and seeking refuge encompasses both together. For the one who seeks refuge is covered by his refuge, clinging to it, holding fast to it. His heart has clung to it and stuck to it, as a child clings to his father when his enemy has drawn a sword against him and aimed it at him, so he flees. If his father appears to him on the path of his flight, he throws himself upon him and holds fast to him with the strongest grip. Likewise the one who seeks refuge has fled from his enemy who seeks his destruction to his Lord and Master, has run to Him, cast himself before Him, held fast to Him, and sought His protection.

Furthermore, the meaning of seeking refuge that abides in the heart of the believer goes beyond these expressions.

These are only an image, an indication and an explanation. Otherwise, what arises in the heart at that moment of seeking shelter, holding fast, prostrating before the Lord, neediness toward Him, and humbling oneself before Him is a matter that expression cannot encompass.

A parallel to this is the expression of the meaning of love for Him, fear of Him, reverence for Him and awe of Him. Expression falls short of describing that, and it is not grasped except through experiencing it, not by mere description and report. Just as, if you described the pleasure of intercourse to an impotent man who had never been created with any desire at all, however much you brought it near to him and likened it to whatever you could liken it to, you would not convey the true knowledge of it to his heart. But if you described it to one in whom desire had been created and fixed, he would know it through existence and taste.

The original form of this verb is ʿa'ūdhu with a sukūn on the ʿayn and a ḍamma on the waw. Then it was made to undergo i'lal (morphological weakening) by moving the vowel of the waw to the ʿayn and making the waw quiescent. So they said ʿa'ūdhu according to the basis of this pattern. Then they applied this weakening consistently, and in the active participle they said ʿā'idh. Its original form was ʿāwidh. The waw came after the alif of the active participle pattern, so they changed it to a hamza, as they said qā'im and khā'if. For the verbal noun they said ʿiyādhan billāh (seeking refuge in Allah). Its original form was ʿiwādhan, like ludhūdh (clinging); they changed the waw to a yā' because of the kasra before it, and its own vowel did not protect it because it had been weakened by i'lal in its functioning. And they said mustaʿīdh (one who seeks refuge). Its original form was mustaʿwidh, like mustakhrij, so they moved the kasra of the waw to the ʿayn before it. When the ʿayn became kasra, it took a kasra before it, so it was changed to a yā' according to the basis of the pattern.

If you ask: Why did the sīn and tā' enter the imperative of this verb, as in His saying: ﴿So seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan﴾ (fa-staʿidh billāhi min al-shayṭān al-rajīm), but they did not enter the past and present tenses? Rather, the most common usage is ʿa'ūdhu billāh and taʿawwadhtu, not astaʿīdhu and istaʿadhtu?

I say: The sīn and tā' indicate a request. So your saying astaʿīdhu billāh means: I ask for the refuge of Allah. Just as when you say astakhīru Allāh (I ask Allah to choose for me), that is: I ask for His choosing; and astaghfiru Allāh (I ask Allah's forgiveness), that is: I ask for His forgiveness; and astaqīluhu (I ask Him to pardon me), that is: I ask for His pardon. So the sīn and tā' were included in the verb to signal the request of this meaning from the one who grants refuge. When the one commanded says ʿa'ūdhu billāh, he has complied with what was requested of him, because he was asked to hold fast and seek protection. There is a difference between the act of holding fast and seeking protection itself, and asking for that. Since the one who seeks refuge is fleeing, holding fast and taking refuge in Allah, he brought the verb that indicates this, not the verb that indicates the request for it. So reflect on this.

This is different from when it is said: "Seek forgiveness from Allah," and he says: astaghfiru Allāh. For he was asked to request forgiveness from Allah, and when he says astaghfiru Allāh, he has complied, because the meaning is: I ask Allah to forgive me.

When this meaning is intended in seeking refuge, there is no harm in using the sīn and tā', so one says astaʿīdhu billāh, meaning: I ask Him to grant me refuge. But this is a meaning other than the very act of holding fast, seeking shelter and fleeing to Him.

So the first (ʿa'ūdhu) reports about his state and his seeking refuge with his Lord, and its report includes his request and his asking that He grant him refuge. The second (astaʿīdhu) is one who asks and requests from his Lord that He grant him refuge, as if he were saying: I ask You to grant me refuge.

Thus the state of the first is more complete. For this reason, what came from the Prophet (ﷺ) in complying with this command was: "I seek refuge with Allah from the accursed Satan." And: "I seek refuge in the perfect words of Allah." And: "I seek refuge in the might of Allah and His power." Not astaʿīdhu. Rather, what Allah taught him is to say: ﴿Say: I seek refuge with the Lord of the daybreak﴾ and ﴿I seek refuge with the Lord of mankind﴾, not astaʿīdhu. So reflect on this wondrous wisdom.

If you ask: How did the compliance with this command come in the form of an imperative and the thing commanded, when He said: ﴿Say: I seek refuge with the Lord of the daybreak﴾ and ﴿Say: I seek refuge with the Lord of mankind﴾? It is known that when it is said "Say: Praise be to Allah," and "Say: Glory be to Allah," compliance with it is to say "Praise be to Allah" and "Glory be to Allah," and not to say "Say: Glory be to Allah."

I say: This is the very question that Ubayy ibn Ka'b put to the Prophet (ﷺ), and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) answered him with it.

Al-Bukhari said in his Sahih: Qutayba told us, Sufyan told us, from Asim and Abda, from Zirr ibn Hubaysh, who said: "I asked Ubayy ibn Ka'b about the two refuge surahs. He said: I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said: 'It was said to me, so I said.' So we say what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said." Then he said: Ali ibn Abdullah told us, Sufyan told us, Abda ibn Abi Lubaba told us, from Zirr ibn Hubaysh. And Asim told us, from Zirr, who said: "I asked Ubayy ibn Ka'b. I said: O Abu al-Mundhir, your brother Ibn Mas'ud says such and such. He said: I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said: 'It was said to me, so I said: Say.' So we say what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said."

I say: The object of the verb "to say" is omitted, and its estimate is: "It was said to me: Say," or "It was said to me this wording. So I said as it was said to me."

Under this there is a secret: The Prophet (ﷺ) has in the Qur'an only the duty to convey it. It was not that he composed it himself from his own self; rather, he is the conveyer of it from Allah. And Allah said to him: ﴿Say: I seek refuge with the Lord of the daybreak﴾. So the requirement of complete conveyance was that he say: "Say: I seek refuge with the Lord of the daybreak," as Allah said. And this is the meaning that the Prophet (ﷺ) indicated by his saying: "It was said to me, so I said," meaning: I am not an initiator; rather I am a conveyer. I say as I am told, and I convey the speech of my Lord as He sent it down to me.

So may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him. He conveyed the Message, fulfilled the trust, and said as he was told. This is enough for us against the Mu'tazila (the rationalist school), the Jahmiyya and their brethren who say: "This Arabic Qur'an and this arrangement is speech that he initiated himself." In this hadith is the clearest refutation of this view, and that he (ﷺ) conveyed the speech he was commanded to convey in its form and wording, so that when he was told "Say," he himself said "Say," because he is a pure conveyer. And upon the Messenger is nothing but the conveying.

(Section Two)

On the One in whom refuge is sought. He is Allah alone, Lord of the daybreak, Lord of mankind, King of mankind, God of mankind. It is not fitting to seek refuge in anyone but Him, and refuge is not to be sought in any of His creatures. Rather, He is the One who grants refuge to those who seek it, protects them, and prevents them from the evil of what they sought refuge from. Allah the Exalted has informed in His Book about those who sought refuge in His creatures: that their seeking refuge increased them in transgression and burden. He said, relating about the believing jinn: ﴿And there were men among mankind who sought refuge with men among the jinn, but they only increased them in burden﴾.

It has come in the tafsir (exegesis) that: "A man among the Arabs in the Jahiliyya, when he travelled and the night came upon him in a barren land, would say: 'I seek refuge with the chief of this valley from the evil of the foolish ones of his people.' So he would spend the night in safety and protection from them until morning." So the men increased the jinn by their seeking refuge with their chiefs, in burden, meaning in transgression, sin and evil. They would say: "We have become masters of mankind and the jinn." And "rahaq" (burden) in the speech of the Arabs means sin and violating the sacred prohibitions. So by this seeking refuge they increased them in committing what was forbidden, namely arrogance and self-exaltation, so they thought they had become masters of mankind and the jinn.

The People of the Sunna argued against the Mu'tazila, regarding the view that the words of Allah are not created, by the fact that the Prophet (ﷺ) sought refuge with the words: "I seek refuge in the perfect words of Allah." And he (ﷺ) never seeks refuge in a created thing.

Similar to this is his saying: "I seek refuge in Your pleasure from Your anger, and in Your pardon from Your punishment." This indicates that His pleasure and His pardon are among His attributes, and that they are uncreated. Likewise his saying: "I seek refuge in the might of Allah and His power." And his saying: "I seek refuge in the light of Your face by which the darknesses were illuminated." Whatever the Prophet (ﷺ) sought refuge in is uncreated, for he seeks refuge only in Allah or in one of His attributes.

In these two surahs the seeking of refuge came with the name Lord, King, and God. And lordship in them came attributed to the daybreak and to mankind. And it is necessary that what He described Himself with in these two surahs be suitable to the refuge sought. And the repelling of the evil from which refuge is sought requires the greatest and clearest suitability.

We have established in several places that Allah, glorified is He, is called upon by His Most Beautiful Names, so He is asked for each desired thing by a name that suits it and requires it. The Prophet (ﷺ) said about these two surahs: "No one has sought refuge with the like of them." So the name in which refuge is sought must necessarily require the sought matter, which is repelling the evil from which refuge is sought, or removing it.

This will become established only through the discussion in Section Three, which is the thing from which refuge is sought. Then the suitability mentioned will become clear. So we say:

(Section Three)

On the types of evil from which refuge is sought in these two surahs.

The evil that befalls the servant is of two kinds:

Either sins that he committed, for which he is punished. The occurrence of this is by his own act, intention and effort. This evil is the sins and their consequences. It is the greater of the two evils, the more lasting, and the more closely attached to its possessor.

Or an evil inflicted on him by another. That other is either accountable or not accountable. The accountable is either his counterpart, which is man, or not his counterpart, which is the jinn. The non-accountable are such as the insects and the venomous creatures and others.

Thus these two surahs include seeking refuge from all these evils, in the most concise and comprehensive wording, most indicative of the meaning, and most general in seeking refuge, such that no evil remained that did not enter under the evil from which refuge is sought in them.

The surah of al-Falaq includes seeking refuge from four matters:

The first: the evil of created things, which have evil in general.
The second: the evil of the darkness when it settles.
The third: the evil of those who blow in the knots.
The fourth: the evil of the envier when he envies.

We will speak about these four evils, their occurrences, their connection to the servant, guarding against them before they happen, and by what they are repelled after they happen.

Before discussing that, it is necessary to explain what evil is: what is it, and what is its reality?

We say: "Evil" (sharr) is said of two things: of pain, and of what leads to it.

It has no meaning beyond that. So the evils are the pains and their causes. Thus sins, disbelief, polytheism and the various kinds of injustice are evils, even if their doer gains some purpose and pleasure in them, but they are evils, because they are causes of pains and lead to them, like the leading of all other causes to their effects. The consequence of pain upon them is like the consequence of death upon the taking of deadly poisons, upon slaughter, upon burning by fire, upon strangling with a rope, and other causes that lead to their effects, necessarily, unless an obstacle prevents the causation, or something stronger than the cause and more powerful in demanding its opposite opposes it, as the strength of faith opposes the cause of sins, and the greatness and abundance of the erasing good deeds. So it increases their quantity or quality beyond the causes of punishment, and the stronger repels the weaker.

This is the case with all opposing causes, like the causes of health and sickness, and the causes of weakness and strength.

The point is: these causes in which there is some pleasure are evil, even if the soul attains through them a quick joy. They are like a delicious, appetizing food that is poisoned: when the eater takes it, he finds his eating pleasant and its swallowing agreeable, and after a little while it does to him what it does. Thus it is with sins and transgressions, necessarily, even if the Lawgiver had not informed us of this, for reality, experience, the elite and the common people would be among its greatest witnesses.

Has a blessing ever been removed from anyone except because of the ill effect of his disobedience? When God bestows a blessing upon a servant, He preserves it for him and does not change it away from him until the servant himself strives to change it away from himself: ﴿Indeed, God does not change the condition of a people until they change what is in themselves. And when God intends misfortune for a people, there is no repelling it, and they have no protector apart from Him﴾ [13:11].

﴿That is because God would never change a blessing He had bestowed upon a people until they change what is in themselves﴾ [8:53].

Whoever reflects upon what God has related in His Book about the nations from whom He removed His blessings will find that the cause of all of it is nothing but opposing His command and disobeying His messengers.

Likewise, whoever considers the circumstances of the people of his own age, and what God has removed from them of His blessings, will find that all of it stems from the evil consequences of sins, as it has been said:

*When you are in blessing, then guard it,*
*for sins remove blessings.*

Blessings of God are never preserved by anything like obedience to Him, nor is increase attained in them by anything like gratitude to Him, and blessings are never removed from a servant by anything like disobedience to his Lord. For sin is the fire of blessings: it consumes them just as fire consumes dry firewood. Whoever travels in thought through the conditions of the world needs no one to inform him of this.

The point is that these causes are evils, inevitably.

As for their effects being evils: they are pains of the soul and body. Upon their possessor there gather, together with the intensity of sensory pain, the pain of the spirit through worries, distress, sorrows, and regrets. If the intelligent, discerning person were to grasp this with a true grasp, he would give it its due of caution and earnest effort to flee. But a veil of heedlessness has been cast over his heart, so that God may accomplish a matter that was to be done. Were he to awaken with a true awakening, his soul would be torn apart in this world from regret over what he had missed of his share, both immediate and deferred, from God. This becomes truly manifest to him only at the moment of departing this world, when he is brought near to and gains sight of the world of permanence. Then he will say:

﴿O, would that I had sent forth [good deeds] for my life!﴾ [89:24], and ﴿Alas, my regret over what I neglected concerning God!﴾ [39:56].

Since evil consists of pains and their causes, all of the Prophet's (ﷺ) seekings of refuge revolve around these two foundations.

Everything from which he sought refuge, or which he commanded others to seek refuge from, is either painful or a cause leading to pain. He used to seek refuge at the end of prayer from four things, and he commanded that refuge be sought from them: "the punishment of the grave and the punishment of the Fire." These two are the greatest of painful things, and "the trial of life and death, and the trial of the False Messiah (al-Masih al-Dajjal)." These two are the cause of painful punishment.

So trial is the cause of punishment. He mentioned trial specifically and mentioned both kinds of trial, because it is either in life or after death. The trial of life may be followed by punishment after a delay of time, whereas the trial after death is immediately followed by punishment without delay.

Thus the seeking of refuge returns to seeking refuge from pain and punishment and their causes.

This is among the most emphatic supplications in prayer, to the extent that some of the earlier (salaf) and later (khalaf) scholars required repeating the prayer for one who did not make this supplication in the final tashahhud (testimony of faith). Ibn Hazm made it obligatory in every tashahhud, and said that if one did not say it in it, his prayer was invalid.

Among these is his (ﷺ) saying: "O God, I seek refuge in You from anxiety and sorrow, from incapacity and laziness, from cowardice and miserliness, from the burden of debt and the domination of men."

He sought refuge from eight things, each two of which are paired.

Anxiety and sorrow are a pair, and both are pains and torments of the spirit. The difference between them is that anxiety is the anticipation of evil in the future, while sorrow is the suffering over the occurrence of something disliked in the past, or the loss of something beloved. Both are pain and torment that come upon the spirit. If it relates to the past it is called sorrow, and if it relates to the future it is called anxiety.

Incapacity and laziness are a pair, and both are causes of pain, because they entail the loss of what is beloved. Incapacity entails lack of ability, and laziness entails lack of will. So the spirit suffers for its loss in proportion to its attachment to it and its delight in attaining it if it were achieved.

Cowardice and miserliness are a pair, because both entail the absence of benefit from wealth and body. Both are causes of pain, because the coward misses out on great beloved, joyful, and pleasurable things that are attained only through giving and courage, and miserliness prevents him from them. These two traits are among the greatest causes of pain.

The burden of debt and the domination of men are a pair. Both are painful to the self and torment it. The first is domination by right, which is the burden of debt; the second is domination by wrong, which is the domination of men.

Also: the burden of debt is generally a domination caused by the servant himself, whereas the domination of men is a domination not by his choice.

Among these is his (ﷺ) seeking refuge "from sinfulness and from debt," for both cause immediate pain.

Among these also is his saying: "I seek refuge in Your pleasure from Your anger, and in Your pardon from Your punishment." Anger is the cause of pain, and punishment is pain. So he sought refuge from the greatest pains and their strongest causes.

(Section)

The evil from which refuge is sought is of two kinds. One is existent, and its removal is sought. The other is non-existent, and its remaining non-existent is sought, that it not come to be. Just as absolute good is of two kinds: one is existent, and its continuance, its stability, and its not being taken away is sought; the other is non-existent, and its coming into being and attainment is sought.

These four are the foundational aims of those who ask of the Lord of the worlds, and upon them their requests revolve.

These four aims have come in the words of God, relating the supplication of His servants at the end of Al 'Imran, in their saying: ﴿Our Lord, indeed we heard a caller calling to faith, "Believe in your Lord," so we believed. Our Lord, forgive us our sins and remove from us our misdeeds﴾ [3:193]. This request is for repelling existent evil, for sins and misdeeds are evil, as has been explained. Then He said:

﴿And cause us to die among the righteous﴾ [3:193]. This is a request for the continuance of existent good, which is faith, until He causes them to die upon it. These are two kinds.

Then He said: ﴿Our Lord, and grant us what You promised us through Your messengers﴾ [3:194]. This is a request for non-existent good, that He grant it to them.

Then He said: ﴿And do not disgrace us on the Day of Resurrection﴾ [3:194]. This is a request that non-existent evil not befall them, which is disgrace on the Day of Resurrection.

Thus the two verses comprise the four aims in the most excellent arrangement, ordered in the most excellent sequence. In them, the two kinds that pertain to this world are mentioned first, namely forgiveness and the continuance of Islam until death. Then they are followed by the two kinds that pertain to the Hereafter: that they be given what was promised them through His messengers, and that He not disgrace them on the Day of Resurrection.

Having understood this:

His (ﷺ) saying in the tashahhud of the khutbah (sermon): "And we seek refuge in God from the evils of our souls and the bad consequences of our deeds" encompasses seeking refuge from the evil of the self, which is non-existent but present within it potentially. So one asks that it be repelled and that it not come into being.

As for his saying "from the bad consequences of our deeds," there are two opinions.

One is that it is a seeking of refuge from bad deeds that have already occurred. Thus the hadith encompasses both kinds of seeking refuge: from the non-existent evil that has not yet come to be, and from existent evil. One asks for the repelling of the former and the removal of the latter.

The second opinion is that the bad consequences of deeds are their punishments and their harmful results, which distress their doer. According to this, seeking refuge from them is also a seeking of repelling the effect.

The first is repelling the cause, so he has sought refuge from the occurrence of pain and its causes.

According to the first opinion, attributing "bad consequences" to "deeds" is an attribution of species to genus, since deeds are a genus and their bad consequences are a species of them.

According to the first opinion, attributing "bad consequences" to "deeds" is an attribution of species to genus, since deeds are a genus and their bad consequences are a species of them.

According to the second opinion, it is an attribution of effect to its cause, and of the caused to its cause, as if he had said: "from the punishment of my deeds." Both opinions are possible.

So consider which of them is more fitting to the hadith and more deserving of it. Each of them has a kind of preference. The first is preferred because the origin of bad deeds is the evil of the self: the evil of the self generates bad deeds. So he sought refuge from the quality of the self and from the deeds that arise from that quality. These two comprise the totality of evil and the causes of every pain. Whoever is protected from both is protected from evil in its entirety.

The second is preferred because the bad consequences of deeds are the punishments that distress the doer, and their causes are the evil of the self. So he sought refuge from punishments, pains, and their causes.

The two opinions are, in reality, mutually implicating: seeking refuge from one entails seeking refuge from the other.

(Section)

Since evil has a cause, which is its source, and it has a locus and an endpoint, and since the cause is either from the servant's own essence or from outside, and its locus and endpoint are either himself or others, there are four matters: evil whose source is from himself and which returns to himself at times and to others at other times; and evil whose source is from another, which is its cause, and which returns to himself at times and to others at other times.

The Prophet (ﷺ) gathered these four stations in the supplication taught by al-Siddiq (ﷺ)[^1] (may God be pleased with him), which he should say in the morning, in the evening, and when he lies down: "O God, Originator of the heavens and the earth, Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, Lord and Sovereign of all things, I bear witness that there is no god but You. I seek refuge in You from the evil of my self and the evil of Satan and his association, and that I commit evil against myself, or bring it upon a Muslim."

He mentioned the two sources of evil, which are the self and Satan, and he mentioned its two locuses and endpoints, which are its return to the self or to his Muslim brother. Thus the hadith gathered the sources and locuses of evil in the most concise, comprehensive, and clear wording.

(Section)

Having understood this, let us speak about the evils from which refuge is sought in these two surahs.

The first evil is the general one in His saying: ﴿from the evil of what He created﴾ [113:2]. Here "what" (ma) is merely a relative pronoun. In the verse, evil is attributed to the created object, the thing acted upon, not to the creating of the Lord, exalted is He, which is His act and His bringing into being, for evil does not attach to it in any way. Evil does not enter into any of His attributes or His acts, just as it does not reach His essence, blessed and exalted is He. His essence possesses absolute perfection, in which there is no deficiency in any respect, and His attributes likewise possess absolute perfection and complete majesty, with no defect or deficiency in any way. Likewise His acts are all pure goods, with no evil in them at all. Had He done evil, glory be to Him, a name would have been derived for Him from it, and His names would not all be most beautiful, and a ruling would have returned to Him from it. Exalted is our Lord and sanctified above that.

What He does of justice to His servants, and the punishment of those who deserve punishment among them, is pure good, since it is pure justice and wisdom, and it is evil only in relation to them. So evil occurs in its relation to them and its subsistence in them, not in His act subsisting in Him, exalted is He. We do not deny that evil exists in His created effects, for He is the Creator of good and evil.

But there are two matters that should be kept in mind:

The first: what is evil, or includes evil, is only a separate created effect; it is not an attribute of Him, nor one of His acts.

The second: its being evil is a relative, comparative matter. It is good from the standpoint of the Lord's act and His bringing it into being, and evil from the standpoint of its relation to whoever is evil in regard to it. It has two aspects: from one of them it is good, and that is the aspect in which it is attributed to the Creator, exalted and glorified is He, as creation, bringing into being, and will, because of the profound wisdom it contains, the knowledge of which He has reserved for Himself, and of which He has informed whomever of His creation He wished. Most people's minds are too narrow to grasp the first principles of knowing it, let alone its reality. It suffices them to have general faith that God, glory be to Him, is the Self-Sufficient, the Praiseworthy. And the doer of evil does not do it except out of need, which contradicts His self-sufficiency, or out of deficiency and defect, which contradicts His praiseworthiness. Thus it is impossible for evil to proceed from the Self-Sufficient, the Praiseworthy, as an act,

even though He is the Creator of good and evil.

You have understood that its being evil is a relative matter, and that in itself it is good from the standpoint of its attribution to its Creator and Originator. So do not be heedless of this point, for it opens for you a great door of knowing and loving the Lord. It removes from you doubts in which the minds of most of the eminent have been bewildered.

I have expounded this in the book *al-Tuhfa al-Makkiyya* and the book *al-Fath al-Qudsi*, and other works.

If this is unclear to you, I will clarify it for you with examples.

The first example: when a thief's hand is cut off, the cutting is evil in relation to him, but pure good in relation to people in general, because it protects their wealth and averts harm from them. It is good in relation to the one who orders and decrees the cutting, because it is a kindness to His servants in general, by destroying this harmful limb that injures them. Thus He is praised for His ruling on this, and His command to do it is thanked, deserving praise from His servants, their commendation, and their love.

Likewise is the ruling to kill one who attacks their lives and sanctities, and to flog one who attacks their honor. If this is the punishment of one who attacks their worldly affairs, how much more the punishment of one who attacks their religion and stands between them and the guidance with which God sent His messengers, and which He made the happiness of His servants in their livelihood and their hereafter depend upon? Is there not, in punishing this aggressor, pure good, wisdom, justice, and kindness to the servants? And it is evil in relation to the aggressive transgressor.

So the evil is what subsists in him of that punishment. As for what is attributed to the Lord of it, namely the will, the intention, and the act, it is the very essence of good and wisdom.

So do not let your veil thicken against understanding this great matter, and the secret that informs you about the question of divine decree (qadar), opens the way for you to God, and to knowledge of His wisdom, His mercy, and His kindness to His creatures. And that He, glory be to Him, is as He is the Pious, the Merciful, the Loving, the Benevolent, so He is also the Wise, the Sovereign, the Just. His wisdom does not contradict His mercy. Rather, He places His mercy, His piety, and His kindness in their proper place, and He places His punishment, His justice, His vengeance, and His might in their proper place. Both are demanded by His might and His wisdom, and He is the Mighty, the Wise. It does not befit His wisdom to place His good pleasure and His mercy where punishment and wrath belong, nor to place His wrath and punishment where His good pleasure and mercy belong.

Do not turn to the words of one whose veil has thickened against God, who says: "Both matters are equal in relation to Him, and there is no difference at all; it is pure will without cause or wisdom."

Reflect on the Qur'an from beginning to end, and see how it suffices to refute this claim, and to denounce it most severely, and to declare the Lord Himself free of it. Such as His saying: ﴿Shall We treat those who submit like the criminals? What is wrong with you? How do you judge?﴾ [68:35–36].

And His saying: ﴿Or do those who commit evil deeds think that We will treat them like those who believe and do righteous deeds, equal in their living and their dying? Evil is what they judge﴾ [45:21].

And His saying: ﴿Or shall We treat those who believe and do righteous deeds like corrupters on earth? Or shall We treat the righteous like the wicked?﴾ [38:28].

Thus He denounced the one who thought such an evil thought of Him, and declared Himself free of it.

This shows that it is established in sound natures and minds that this does not occur, nor does it befit His wisdom, His might, and His divinity: there is no god but Him, exalted far above what the ignorant say.

God has created the minds of His servants to find it ugly to place punishment and vengeance where mercy and kindness belong, and to repay a good deed with its like or more. When punishment is placed where kindness belongs, their natures and minds reject it most strongly and find it most repugnant.

Likewise, placing kindness, mercy, and honor where punishment and vengeance belong: if one came to someone who harms the world in every kind of harm, in their wealth, their women, and their lives, and he honored him to the utmost, raised him and ennobled him, natures and minds refuse to approve of this, and testify to the foolishness of the one who did it. This is the natural disposition of God upon which He created people.

What then is the matter with minds and natures that do not witness His profound wisdom, His might, and His justice in placing His punishment in the most worthy places and the most deserving of punishment? And that if blessings were bestowed upon such people, they would not be fitting for them, nor well placed, and the contradiction of wisdom would appear, as the poet said:

*The blessing of God is not to be faulted, but*
*it may be found ugly when given to certain people.*

Thus the blessings of God are not fitting, nor good, nor becoming for His enemies who turn away from His path and strive against His good pleasure, who are pleased when He is angry, and angry when He is pleased, who nullify what He has decreed, and strive to make the call be to other than Him, the rule belong to other than Him, and obedience be to other than Him. They oppose Him in everything He wills. They love what He hates and call to it, and hate what He loves and shun it, and they befriend His enemies, the most hateful of creatures to Him, and support them against Him and His messenger, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And the disbeliever is ever a helper against his Lord﴾ [25:55]. And He said: ﴿And when We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam," they prostrated, except Iblis; he was of the jinn, so he defied the command of his Lord. Will you then take him and his descendants as allies instead of Me, while they are enemies to you?﴾ [18:50].
